serial_correlation.note: record treated as one continuous serially-correlated series

period_scan.design: [1, t, cos(wt), sin(wt), cos(2wt), sin(2wt)], w = 2*pi/P
period_scan.r2_definition: full 6-column design; fundamental amp/phase from cos/sin columns

explanation: The two shipped age models differ on exactly 52 of 621 rows, all in the top 0.55 m (8.29% of the 6.27 m depth span, 8.37% of rows, ages 1.98-32.68 ka); every one of those rows carries d18O, and the two coordinates agree to <= 0.005 ka on all 569 other rows (max |diff| below 0.55 m = 0.0000 ka). The record-wide dominant sinusoid is therefore the same feature under either coordinate: best period 108.835 ka (age_1) vs 108.770 ka (age_2), a shift of 0.065 ka << the ~14 ka age spacing of the ~26 effective samples implied by rho = 0.92; R^2 differs by 0.0046 (0.4273 vs 0.4320) and the fundamental amplitude by 0.0016 per mille, i.e. 0.42% of the amplitude. The constant-rate synthetic coordinate (age = depth/mean_LSR, mean LSR = 0.022345 m/ka) peaks at 84.070 ka with R^2 = 0.4505 and explains only R^2 = 0.0730 at the shipped-coordinate optimum 108.8 ka, so a deliberately uniform age model would relocate the peak to a different period; that is a genuine sensitivity to the age-depth warp as a whole, but it is NOT the choice between the two shipped coordinates, which share 91.7% of their rows and differ only in the top 8% of the depth span. np.gradient LSR is bit-identical between the two coordinates for every row deeper than 0.56 m (array_equal = True, n = 568 rows); the only nonzero gradient differences (max 0.0135 m/ka) are confined to the top 0.56 m, i.e. the divergent interval plus the single-row np.gradient stencil guard. Conclusion: the choice of shipped age coordinate cannot change the record-wide spectral result; it perturbs only the top ~8% of the record locally.
